analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug prices at 6% above the average price in five other industrialized countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor; it sat in two House committees and their subcommittees until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the President to write rules ensuring that no pharmaceutical product is sold to any U.S. consumer for more than 6% above its average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries other than the United States. Companies that overcharged would have faced fines of up to twice the sale amount, and consumers could have sued to recover what they overpaid, plus punitive damages and attorneys' fees, individually or through class actions. The bill was introduced by one representative, attracted no cosponsors, and died in committee without ever receiving a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American who buys a prescription drug. The cap applies to any sale to any consumer in the United States, so uninsured patients paying full sticker price would have benefited most directly. Anyone overcharged could have recovered the amount they paid plus punitive damages and attorneys' fees in court, individually or through a class action. The bill also gave enforcers subpoena power to examine company pricing records, with trade secrets kept confidential.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the price of any pharmaceutical product sold to a U.S. consumer at no more than 6% above its average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries other than the United States, with the President setting the definitions, procedures, and reporting requirements.

Lets the government recover money collected above the cap through court-ordered restitution and civil penalties of up to 200% of a violator's unjust enrichment, counting each overpriced sale as a separate violation.
Adds criminal fines of up to 200% of the sale amount for knowingly violating the price rules.
Gives consumers a private right to sue for what they overpaid plus punitive damages and attorneys' fees, including through class actions with no minimum individual recovery required.
Gives the enforcing officer subpoena power to examine company books and pricing records, with testimony under oath and court-backed enforcement of compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. prices would have been pulled down toward the lower levels charged for the same products in comparable countries, with fines up to twice each violating sale and consumer lawsuits on top. The bill's own findings acknowledge that producers 'must be appropriately compensated,' but it offers no offsetting support for the research those revenues fund. Consumers could also pay indirectly over the long run if lower expected prices mean fewer new drugs developed.

drawbacks.text: The bill hands sweeping power to a single office: the President decides which products count, how the five-country average is calculated, and can compromise or remit penalties — so enforcement would rise or fall with whoever occupies the White House.

Capping U.S. prices at foreign levels would cut drug-company revenue with no replacement funding for research and development, a tradeoff the bill does not address even while conceding producers must be compensated.

The enforcement design is blunt: every overpriced sale is a separate violation carrying criminal exposure of up to twice the sale amount, a scheme that could entangle retailers and pharmacists, not just manufacturers, and computing an 'average retail price' across five countries with different products, pack sizes, and currencies would be contentious.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit would have been real and large — the bill's findings concede that pricing 'varies greatly from country to country,' and tying U.S. prices to what peer countries charge is exactly how the gap gets closed. But the bill was a blunt instrument: it delegated price-setting to the President with few guardrails, relied on criminal and punitive penalties on a per-sale basis, and said nothing about protecting the research funding it would take from drug makers. A better-designed version would pair the cap with sustained support for drug development and clearer enforcement standards. As introduced, the idea was sounder than the drafting.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors, it was referred to two House committees, then passed down to one subcommittee in each, and neither subcommittee ever acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens (D-NY) introduced the Pharmaceutical Products Price Equity Act in the House on February 5, 2003.
The House referred it to two committees at once — Energy and Commerce and the Judiciary — splitting jurisdiction over the bill between them.

In February and March 2003 the bill was sent down to a subcommittee in each committee — the Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection Subcommittee and the Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property Subcommittee — the level where most bills go to stall.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or cosponsor ever followed; the bill attracted zero cosponsors from either party.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill died with the subcommittee referrals as its last action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, which kept charging U.S. prices with no link to what the same medicines cost abroad. U.S. consumers who buy prescriptions gained nothing, and no alternative price-relief bill from Rep. Owens advanced in its place.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 5, 2003; it never attracted a single cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or a committee vote after its referral; it was passed down to a subcommittee on February 14, 2003, and never came back.

against.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action after its referral; it was sent to the intellectual property subcommittee on March 6, 2003, and died there.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price controls on prescription drugs and lobbied against them throughout this period; no action on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so its fate was decided by committee inaction, not by a floor test.

industries.note: The bill would cap U.S. retail prices at roughly the average charged in five peer countries, with fines up to twice each violating sale and consumer class actions for overcharges. The United States is the industry's largest and highest-price market, so the cap would cut its biggest source of revenue — which is precisely the money ordinary patients would save.
